results.title: Introducing our Training API
results.author: Kailash Ranganathan, Micah Yong
highlights:
Introducing our Training API

 Kailash Ranganathan Micah Yong

 Oct 22, 2026 

# Introducing our Training API

Thinking Machines’ Tinker changed how people do post-training. You write the training loop in plain Python on your laptop, and Tinker runs the forward and backward passes on its GPUs. We’re big fans, and so are many of the teams we work with.

As those teams scale up, however, they keep raising the same two problems:

1. Per-token pricing gets expensive once you’re running dozens of experiments.
2. You can only use the models and features the provider decides to support.

We think a good API deserves more than one implementation. Today we’re releasing Spindle, an open-source, Tinker-compatible training server that runs in your Modal workspace. Because you own the server, you can customize anything in it, and you pay for GPU time instead of tokens. Our default configs are tuned to maximize GPU utilization out of the box, and we plan to keep shipping optimizations to push price-performance further.

All it takes is a single command to deploy a server:

```
spindle deploy

...

Then, run your training script against the server.

...

You write the training loop with your own losses, rewards, and environments, and Spindle handles the distributed training underneath it. It supports full-parameter training and multi-LoRA on a wide range of open models. For teams running many experiments, Spindle supports hundreds of concurrent training runs at similar performance and significantly reduced cost compared to closed-source APIs.

...

Spindle’s multi-LoRA backend puts trainer idle time to work by letting many clients share the same trainer. While one client waits on rollouts, the trainer runs another client’s training step. When several clients share the same GPUs, each run costs a fraction of what it would on dedicated compute.

To quantify this, consider the same simple GRPO job (a 27B model on DAPO-math) with one to eight clients sharing the same trainer and inference GPUs (4×H200s for training, 12×B200s for inference).

Looking at the trainer’s utilization, we can see where the cost benefits come from:

With a single client, the trainer has long idle periods. With four clients interleaving their training steps, it stays ~88% busy. Adding clients lowers the cost of each run, at the expense of each run finishing a bit more slowly. Note that there is a limit: past four clients here, we observe thrashing of the trainer which significantly degrades per-client throughput.

The same effect scales to agentic workloads. Here are some workloads we ran on Spindle, from single-turn math to long-horizon agents, each compared with running the same script on Tinker:

| Workload | Setup | Clients | $/1M output tokens | Price reduction vs. Tinker |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DAPO-math, single-turn (Qwen3.8-27B) | Tinker | 1 | $9.77 | — |
| | Spindle: 4×H200 train, 12×B200 inference | 2 | $3.57 | −63% |
| | Spindle: 8×H200 train, 8×H200 inference | 8 | $1.99 | −80% |
| Search agent, up to 40 turns (gpt-oss-20b) | Tinker | 1 | $5.06 | — |
| | Spindle: 8×H200 train, 16×H200 inference | 4 | $4.06 | −20% |
| | Spindle: 8×H200 train, 16×H200 inference | 8 | $3.80 | −25% |
| SWE-Gym, 256K context (Qwen3.8-27B) | Tinker | — | $15.04 | — |
| | Spindle: 8×B200 train, 8×B200 inference | 4 | $6.17 | −59% |
| | Spindle: 8×B200 train, 12×B200 inference | 8 | $5.82 | −61% |

Paying for the GPUs instead of tokens means every bit of extra throughput you get out of them lowers your price per token. The broader takeaway from these experiments is that if you keep your GPUs busy, for example by running several experiments at once, Spindle offers much better price-performance than closed-source APIs.

...

We’re still in beta, and we’re cooking up performance optimizations, improved autoscaling, new features and training recipes, and much more. Stay tuned and happy Spindling! 🍽️

results.title: Endpoint Candidates: evaluate and promote inference endpoints
results.author: Amit Lohe, Adhvik Kanagala, Deven Navani, Garrett O'Brien
highlights:
Endpoint Candidates: evaluate and promote inference endpoints

 Oct 12, 2026 

# Endpoint Candidates: evaluate and promote inference endpoints

Latency, throughput, and cost optimization are at the core of modern inference engineering. Without testing and measurement, these metrics cannot be reliably improved.

We’ve been focused on inference performance for some time now, and we’re building several new tools to help you optimize your own inference servers–starting with Endpoint Candidates.

Endpoint Candidates allow you to stage alternative deployments for your Dedicated Endpoints, so you can evaluate the impact on quality, latency, throughput, and cost. Each Candidate can mirror production, handling a sample of production traffic while Modal runs the underlying infrastructure. When you’re ready, promote your Candidate to production from the dashboard.

...

Endpoint Candidates use standard Modal compute pricing, including compute used for mirrored requests.

results.title: Modal Clusters are generally available
results.author: Peyton Walters
highlights:
Modal Clusters are generally available

 Peyton Walters Oct 1, 2026 

# Modal Clusters are generally available

Organizations need to own their intelligence to be successful. Training and serving that intelligence at scale, however, requires petaFLOP/s of compute and terabit/s of networking, spread across many nodes. But owning intelligence doesn’t need to mean owning that hardware.

For the past 1.5 years, we’ve been battle-testing a new primitive: Modal Clusters. Today, we’re excited to announce that they are generally available through a single decorator, `@modal.clustered`:

...

Modal Clusters seamlessly integrate with all existing Modal primitives. Write your checkpoints to Volumes, load data in through Cloud Bucket Mounts, and orchestrate your jobs with Queues. On top of existing integration, you get:

- Communication between nodes via InfiniBand verbs at up to 6.4 Tbps, automatically configured for PyTorch and NCCL
- Your code running on a cluster within seconds of requesting it, billed by the second
- Our robust, automated GPU health assurance and remediation, now extended to RDMA health

Elsewhere, on-demand cluster access means paying by the hour or taking a reservation. On Modal, you run whenever you want and only pay for what you use.

...

The gang scheduler pulls from the same capacity pool as everything else on Modal, allowing for cluster acquisition in seconds. This is the fastest time to get a multi-node cluster on the market, and the only place where you pay truly serverless pricing.

...

Modal Clusters are available to all workspaces today. Whether you’re scaling out inference or post-training a frontier model, all it takes is one line of code to scale out your Modal App. Cluster size is bounded by your plan’s GPU limits, so if you’re planning something big, reach out.

results.title: How Snorkel runs realistic agent simulations with Modal
highlights:
Nov 6, 2026

...

## Decreasing costs by 20% with memory bursting

Previously, the Snorkel team was estimating the CPU and memory needs of their agents when configuring a sandbox. In some cases, the agent would fail because the sandbox didn’t have sufficient resources to complete the task, rendering the result of the run invalid. In other cases, resources were over-provisioned, leading to low spend-efficiency.

Estimating the resource needs of agents is particularly difficult for two reasons: resource usage within a Sandbox is spiky, and workload shapes are not statically known. ... This is especially true for Snorkel because of the large variety of benchmarks they run.

To simplify provisioning, Snorkel began using Modal’s bursting, where individual Sandboxes can elastically expand the memory or CPU resources they need at a given point. Customers are charged for the resources the Sandbox is using at a given time or the resources that were originally requested, whichever is higher. They’re still early in the adoption process, with ~10-15% of Snorkel’s sandboxes using bursting today.

Random sample of 5,000 Snorkel’s Sandboxes plotted by peak CPU and Memory usage as a % of the resource request.

Bursting made it possible to allocate CPU and memory at configuration while retaining flexibility at runtime. For the Snorkel team, this meant the reliability of runs increased as the number of runs failing due to resource limits decreased. Bursting also allowed Snorkel to lower the amount of resources they were requesting for their Sandboxes without compromising reliability— leading to substantial cost savings.

> “We need to support tasks from SMEs or agents, without over-provisioning infrastructure. Bursting gives us flexibility at configuration and runtime, avoiding over-provisioning and saving us around 20% on our total Sandbox bill.”

Rustem Feyzkhanov Sr. Manager AI Platform

results.title: VM Sandboxes: Full computers for agents
results.author: Amit Prasad
highlights:
Amit Prasad Oct 1, 2026 

# VM Sandboxes: Full computers for agents

Today we’re making VM Sandboxes generally available on Modal, built for those who need to give their agents the power of a full computer.

...

## So, should I switch everything over?

Short answer: it depends! If your workload runs happily on Modal Sandboxes today, it'll continue running happily on gVisor, which currently remains as our default runtime. 

Reach for `runtime="vm"` when you butt against the walls of userspace: Docker, FUSE filesystems, or niche Linux kernel features. We’ve made switching as simple as flipping a flag, with both runtimes sharing the same APIs, Images, and usage-based pricing.
